Yes indeed, insurance companies are just a layer of bureaucracy between the patient and healthcare provider.

In theory, they should be able to work towards more affordable treatments and encourage efficient practices. However, in reality, no insurance company actually does this. Many offer wellness programs to reduce preventable diseases - but those are the same programs that would be provided by a government-run system. And insurance companies (fortunately) don't have the power to tell hospitals that they will only provide the cheaper treatments. All they can do is negotiate discounts with the hospital, and every company has its own discounts, so as a result no one has any clue what the actual cost of a medical procedure is anymore. Hospitals have a master list of all their prices, but they intentionally inflate those prices so they can promise bigger discounts to the insurance companies. If a patient doesn't have insurance, they get a bill for the full inflated amount that no one is actually supposed to pay (the trick here is to call the hospital's billing department and ask for a discount because you aren't a millionaire, and they can/should reduce it to a more realistic price, but few people know this).

It's all a perfect example of what happens when every side competes to squeeze a few more dollars of profit out of a system. They all try to outmaneuver each other, and each spend $100 trying to grab that last $1. It's classic game theory.

When insurance companies began negotiating discounts with healthcare providers and establishing networks, the system was doomed to inefficiency.
